key_insight: PosteriorBench shifts evaluation of generative inverse solvers from “does it produce one good answer?” to “does it match the full posterior distribution?” This reveals failures like mode collapse and overconfident uncertainty that point estimates can hide.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the mismatch between traditional point-estimate evaluation and the needs of ill-posed inverse problems, where many reconstructions can be consistent with the same sparse or noisy measurements.
method: Introduces PosteriorBench, an evaluation framework centered on posterior matching rather than single-sample accuracy.
Compares generative inverse solvers using criteria that reflect distributional correctness, diversity, and uncertainty calibration.
Targets failure modes such as mode collapse, averaged outputs, and overconfident predictions that can still look good under pointwise metrics.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a more realistic way to judge whether inverse solvers are scientifically trustworthy, not just visually plausible. It helps prevent deploying models that look accurate on benchmarks but fail to represent uncertainty correctly in real scientific settings.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: point estimate vs posterior distribution
Flowchart of inverse problem: sparse observation → multiple valid reconstructions

paper_title: PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers
paper_authors: Jiachen Yao, Zi-Siang Hsu, Xi Deng, Aditi Gupta, Xin Ju
